course_title: Ethereum and Solidity: The Complete Developer's Guide

screens.title: Event Handling and Real-time Updates
screens.subtitle: How smart contract events connect the blockchain to responsive frontends

narration.text: Events are the bridge between immutable on-chain processes and dynamic off-chain user interfaces. In this lesson you will learn what Solidity events are, why they matter for DApps, and how to listen for them using Web3. js and Ethers. js. You will see a concrete contract that emits two events, one for value changes and one for ownership transfers, and then follow a terminal-style demo showing a listener script that prints events in real time. This matters because polling the chain is slow and wasteful; subscriptions using a WebSocket provider let a UI react immediately when something important happens on-chain. We'll also cover indexed parameters, which let nodes store topics that you can efficiently filter by, and practical safety notes such as unsubscribing and converting BigNumber types before rendering. By the end you’ll understand how to wire a contract event into a live frontend, what to do when a connection drops, and how to avoid common mistakes. Think about this: when your contract emits an event, what single UI element would you update first in your DApp?

keyIdea.title: Events enable reactive DApps
keyIdea.text: Solidity events record important transaction details in logs so off-chain listeners can subscribe, filter, and update UIs in real time without inefficient polling.

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define and emit events in Solidity, subscribe to those events using both Web3. js and Ethers. js, and filter event streams by indexed parameters. You will practice converting event data types for display and wiring listeners into a frontend to update state in real time. You will also implement essential safety patterns: using a WebSocket provider for live updates, unsubscribing when components unmount, and handling provider errors and reconnection attempts. Each objective maps to a practical milestone, such as deploying the EventfulContract to a local test node, writing a listener script that logs events, filtering for a specific address, and demonstrating a graceful reconnection after a WebSocket interruption. These skills let you build responsive DApps that react to on-chain activity without heavy polling. Keep an eye on data parsing: numeric values may arrive as BigNumber types and require conversion before rendering.

screens.title: What is a Solidity event?
screens.subtitle: A contract's way to broadcast structured logs for off-chain listeners

narration.text: A Solidity event is a language feature that lets a contract record a named log entry when something important happens. When a contract emits an event, that information goes into the transaction receipt's logs, which Ethereum nodes index and expose to external clients. Events contain parameters, and up to three of those parameters can be marked indexed, which stores them in topics for efficient node-side filtering. For a DApp, the practical meaning is straightforward: the contract cannot push a message directly to a browser, but it can emit an event that a listener receives and reacts to. A concrete example from our source contract is ValueChanged, emitted with the setter address, oldValue, and newValue. When your frontend subscribes, it receives that event and can update a displayed value, notify a user, or trigger further queries. A common misconception is to treat events as contract state; they are logs — historically useful records — and not a replacement for reading contract storage. The takeaway is to use events for notifications and indexing, while keeping authoritative state reads on-chain where needed. How might you balance a UI that shows an optimistic update from an event versus one that re-reads state from the contract?

keyIdea.title: Event = logged notification
keyIdea.text: Events are stored in transaction logs, are indexed by nodes, and serve as efficient notifications to off-chain listeners, not as on-chain state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › What is a Solidity event?
Definition and meaning
A compact definition and practical implications for DApps.
Formal claim
Events record structured data in transaction logs that external nodes index and expose to clients.
Concrete example
ValueChanged(address indexed setter, uint oldValue, uint newValue) — emitted when the owner updates a stored value.
Key Takeaway

Use events as notifications for listeners; verify state with on-chain reads if you need authoritative values.

Annotated example
event ValueChanged(address indexed setter, uint oldValue, uint newValue);

function setValue(uint _newValue) public {
  require(msg.sender == owner);
  emit ValueChanged(msg.sender, value, _newValue);
  value = _newValue;
}
Indexed parameter
setter is indexed so nodes can filter by this address efficiently.
Non-indexed data
oldValue and newValue are in the event data but not in topics if unindexed.
Common misconception
Events are not a substitute for contract storage. They provide historical logs and are great for notifications, but you must read storage for authoritative state.

screens.title: Defining and Emitting Events in Solidity
screens.subtitle: Walk through EventfulContract and its emitted events

narration.text: Let's inspect the contract you will deploy. The EventfulContract declares two events: ValueChanged and OwnershipTransferred. ValueChanged carries the setter address and numeric values for old and new state, while OwnershipTransferred records an ownership handoff between two addresses. Notice the use of the emit keyword to create a log entry. When setValue is called by the owner, the contract first emits ValueChanged with the caller, the current value, and the new value, and then updates storage. This ordering is important if listeners rely on the event to reflect the former value. The contract uses the indexed modifier on address parameters so listeners can filter efficiently by those addresses. A concrete deployment checklist: compile with the same Solidity version, deploy to Ganache, copy the ABI and contract address, and add that address to your listener script. A common mistake is including sensitive data in events; remember that event logs are public and permanent. Another pitfall is assuming events are immediately available to all nodes; listeners should handle reorgs and confirmatory logic if your DApp requires absolute finality. As you read this code, ask yourself which UI updates can be optimistic from an event and which should wait for a storage read.

keyIdea.title: Emit before state change
keyIdea.text: Emitting an event before or after storage updates affects what listeners infer—decide intentionally and document the contract behavior.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Emitting Events
EventfulContract.sol (excerpt)
// SPDX-License-Identifier: MIT
pragma solidity ^0.8.0;

contract EventfulContract {
    address public owner;
    uint public value;

    event ValueChanged(address indexed setter, uint oldValue, uint newValue);
    event OwnershipTransferred(address indexed previousOwner, address indexed newOwner);

    constructor() { owner = msg.sender; value = 0; }

    function setValue(uint _newValue) public {
        require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can set value");
        emit ValueChanged(msg.sender, value, _newValue);
        value = _newValue;
    }
}
Annotations
  • Indexed addresses: used for node-level filtering and appear in topics.
  • Emit order: emitting before storage updates can show prior state in an event.
  • Ownership event: index both previous and new owner to filter transfers by either address.
Concrete example
When the owner calls setValue(10), the contract emits ValueChanged with the setter and the old and new values, then writes the new value to storage. A listener will receive the event and can update the displayed value quickly.
Key Takeaway

Design events intentionally: pick which parameters to index and decide whether emitting occurs before or after storage changes.

screens.title: Indexed Parameters and Event Filtering
screens.subtitle: How indexed fields become topics for efficient queries

narration.text: Indexed parameters are the key to efficient event queries. When you mark a parameter indexed, the node stores its hashed value in a topic rather than in the event data. Up to three parameters can be indexed. This enables node-level filtering so you can ask for events where that parameter equals a given value without fetching and scanning all logs. For example, marking the setter or newOwner as indexed lets you filter by address at the provider or contract filter level. A concrete contrast: if you try to filter by a non-indexed string parameter, the node cannot help and you must download all matching events and filter client-side, which is slow and resource-intensive. Use indexed parameters for values you expect to filter by, such as addresses or identifiers. However, avoid indexing large dynamic types like strings or long blobs. A common misconception is that indexing stores the parameter in a human-readable field; in fact, topics store hashed or normalized representations and the full value may still be in event data if not indexed. The practical rule: choose up to three indexed parameters you will filter on and keep the rest unindexed for storage in the event data.

keyIdea.title: Index only what you will filter
keyIdea.text: Indexed parameters become topics that nodes can filter by; use them for addresses and identifiers you will query frequently.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Indexed Parameters
Indexed parameters explained
Why you index, what is stored, and how filtering works in practice.
How nodes store indexed values
Indexed parameters are recorded in topics, enabling provider-side filters that avoid transferring all logs to the client.
Practical tip
Index addresses and numeric IDs you will query. Do not index long strings or private data.
Common mistake

Trying to filter by non-indexed parameters will force client-side scanning. Only index what you'll filter by.

Filter patterns
Web3.js example
contract.events.OwnershipTransferred({ filter: { newOwner: specificAddress } }).on('data', ...)
Ethers.js filter
const filter = contract.filters.OwnershipTransferred(null, specificAddress); contract.on(filter, ...)
Example scenario
If you want to show only transfers to a specific address, index newOwner and create a topic filter. The node will return only matching logs, saving bandwidth and latency.

screens.title: Listening to Events with Web3.js
screens.subtitle: A terminal-style demo using a WebSocket provider

narration.text: Web3. js supports event subscriptions through a contract. events A P I when connected over a WebSocket provider. In practice you create a Web3 instance with a WebsocketProvider, instantiate the contract with its ABI and address, and call contract. events. EventName(). on('data', callback) to receive events as they're emitted. The listener receives event. returnValues containing the parameters and metadata such as blockHash and transactionHash in the full event object. Use. on('error') to catch subscription errors. A concrete snippet from the chapter shows listening to ValueChanged and a filtered OwnershipTransferred where newOwner matches a given address. For reliable long-running listeners, remember to unsubscribe when your application context changes. In Web3. js the subscription returned supports. unsubscribe() to stop streaming. A frequent mistake is using HttpProvider instead of WebSocketProvider: HTTP does not support subscriptions and will not stream new events. When setting up your listener, also ensure you handle reconnects and do not leak multiple listeners in single-page applications. As a quick reflection, consider how to structure a listener module so that it exposes a single subscribe/unsubscribe A P I that UI components can call safely.

keyIdea.title: Web3.js: events() stream
keyIdea.text: Use WebSocketProvider and contract.events.EventName to stream event.returnValues; call unsubscribe when finished to avoid leaks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Web3.js Listener
Terminal-style snippet
const web3Ws = new Web3(new Web3.providers.WebsocketProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:7545'));
const eventfulContract = new web3Ws.eth.Contract(CONTRACT_ABI, CONTRACT_ADDRESS);

eventfulContract.events.ValueChanged()
  .on('data', event => { console.log(event.returnValues); })
  .on('error', error => console.error('ValueChanged Error', error));

const sub = eventfulContract.events.OwnershipTransferred({ filter: { newOwner: specificNewOwner } })
  .on('data', event => console.log('Filtered:', event.returnValues));

// Later: sub.unsubscribe();
Notes
  • Use a WebSocket provider for real-time streams; HTTP does not stream events.
  • Handle errors on the subscription and unsubscribe when done.
  • Filtered subscriptions rely on indexed parameters; non-indexed filters require client-side checking.
Example output
When ValueChanged emits, the listener logs the setter address and the old and new values, which your UI can use to update an input or notification.

screens.title: Listening with Ethers.js and Filters
screens.subtitle: Cleaner APIs and filter objects for indexed parameters

narration.text: Ethers. js offers a concise and robust A P I for event listening. You create a WebSocketProvider, instantiate a Contract, and call contract. on('EventName', handler) to receive events. For filtered listeners by indexed parameters, ethers exposes contract. filters. EventName(... values) which returns a filter object you can pass to contract. on(filter, handler). This is efficient because the filter encodes indexed values for topics and prevents unnecessary log transfer. The chapter shows an example where filter = contract. filters. OwnershipTransferred(null, specificNewOwner) and then the listener receives only those transfers. Ethers' event handler parameters are the event values themselves followed by a full event object that includes blockHash and transactionHash for context. Unlike older patterns, ethers keeps listener management simple with contract. off() to remove handlers. Convert BigNumber values to strings with toString() before rendering; many uints arrive as BigNumber wrappers. Also handle provider events like 'error' and 'close' to log and attempt reconnection. A useful misconception to avoid is thinking contract. on always reconnects for you; implement an exponential backoff reconnection strategy in production systems. As you try this demo, pay attention to the ergonomics: ethers tends to make listener lifecycle easier to reason about.

keyIdea.title: Ethers.js filters
keyIdea.text: Use contract.filters to build topic filters and contract.on(filter) to receive only matching events; remember to convert BigNumber values before display.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Ethers.js Listener
Example snippet
const providerWs = new ethers.providers.WebSocketProvider('ws://127.0.0.1:7545');
const contract = new ethers.Contract(CONTRACT_ADDRESS, CONTRACT_ABI, providerWs);

contract.on('ValueChanged', (setter, oldValue, newValue, event) => {
  console.log('ValueChanged:', setter, oldValue.toString(), newValue.toString());
});

const filter = contract.filters.OwnershipTransferred(null, specificNewOwner);
contract.on(filter, (prevOwner, newOwner, event) => {
  console.log('Filtered transfer:', prevOwner, newOwner);
});

providerWs.on('error', err => console.error('Provider Error', err));
providerWs.on('close', (code, reason) => console.log('WebSocket closed', code, reason));
Notes & best practices
  • Convert BigNumber types with toString() before display.
  • Use filter objects to leverage node-side indexing.
  • Remove listeners with contract.off(filter, handler) or contract.removeAllListeners for cleanup.
Example scenario
If your app needs only events where a particular account is the recipient, create a filter for that account and listen with contract.on(filter) to reduce noise and latency.

screens.title: Polling vs Event-driven Updates
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs between querying state and subscribing to events

narration.text: Polling and event-driven subscriptions are two approaches to keeping a UI in sync with the blockchain. Polling repeatedly calls provider methods like getBlockNumber or contract state getters on a timer. It is simple but inefficient: it sends many requests, increases latency, and wastes node resources. Event-driven updates use a persistent WebSocket connection that streams events and block notifications as they happen. This yields lower latency and less wasted work. However, subscriptions require handling connection stability, reconnection logic, and sometimes provider rate limits. A practical compromise is to use events for immediate UI updates and to run occasional polling or on-demand reads to confirm final state when required. For example, when ValueChanged fires, you can optimistically update the UI and then call contract. value() once to confirm. A common pitfall is relying solely on events for authoritative data; events are logs and can be reordered in rare chain reorganizations. So design your UI to treat events as notifications and confirm critical state with reads. Reflect on your application's tolerance for eventual consistency and choose a pattern that balances responsiveness and correctness.

keyIdea.title: Use both patterns
keyIdea.text: Prefer events for responsiveness and polling or direct reads for authoritative confirmation when finality matters.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Polling vs Events
Polling
Periodic reads such as provider.getBlockNumber or contract methods called on an interval. Simple but wasteful.
  • Pros: easy to implement, works with HTTP providers.
  • Cons: latency on update, extra network load, less responsive UX.
Event-driven
Subscriptions over WebSocket providers that push events and blocks to the client as they occur.
  • Pros: low-latency updates, efficient bandwidth usage.
  • Cons: requires WebSocket connections and reconnection logic.
Best practice
Use events for immediate UI feedback, then optionally confirm important values with a direct on-chain read. This pattern balances responsiveness and correctness while keeping network use reasonable.

screens.title: Handling Provider Errors and Reconnection
screens.subtitle: Strategies to keep event listeners robust in production

narration.text: WebSocket connections can and will disconnect. To build a robust listener you must detect errors, attempt reconnection with backoff, and ensure no duplicate handlers are added after reconnect. The recommended process starts with creating a single provider instance and a single contract listener. Listen for provider-level events such as error and close, log them, and start a reconnection routine that waits progressively longer between attempts. When reconnecting, reinstantiate the provider and reattach your contract listeners, but make sure you first remove old listeners to avoid duplicates. In single-page applications, unsubscribe when a component unmounts to prevent memory leaks, for example using Web3. js's unsubscribe or Ethers. js's contract. off in a cleanup callback. Another practical detail is to replay missed events after reconnect by querying past events from the last known block number to the current head. This ensures you do not miss updates while disconnected. A common mistake is to restart listeners without clearing state, causing handlers to fire multiple times. Design your listener lifecycle with explicit start, stop, and reconnect states for clarity. Handling Provider Errors and Reconnection means implement exponential backoff, replay missed events by querying past events, and remove old listeners before reattaching to avoid duplicate callbacks.. In practical terms, strategies to keep event listeners robust in production. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Reconnect and dedupe
keyIdea.text: Implement exponential backoff, replay missed events by querying past events, and remove old listeners before reattaching to avoid duplicate callbacks.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Error Handling
Lifecycle steps
  1. Start provider and attach single listener instance.
  2. On provider error or close, log and trigger reconnect logic with backoff.
  3. Before reattaching, remove existing listeners to avoid duplication.
  4. After reconnect, query past events from lastKnownBlock to head to replay missed items.
  5. Expose unsubscribe so UI components can call cleanup when unmounting.
Quick checklist
  • Implement exponential backoff for reconnection.
  • Keep a lastSeenBlock to replay events.
  • Remove listeners before reattaching.
Key Takeaway

Treat subscriptions as managed resources: start, stop, and recover them explicitly and replay missed events after reconnecting.

screens.title: Processing Event Data for Real-time UI Updates
screens.subtitle: Parsing, converting, and integrating event payloads into the frontend

narration.text: Receiving an event is only the first step; you must convert and integrate its data into your UI safely. Numeric types such as uint often arrive as BigNumber objects; call toString or formatUnits as appropriate before updating the DOM. Addresses may need normalization or checksumming before comparison. Design your listener to parse the event. returnValues or the ethers handler parameters into a lightweight JavaScript object with typed fields. Once parsed, decide whether the UI will apply optimistic updates or validate by reading the contract state. For example, when a ValueChanged event arrives, you might immediately update a displayed value and then call the contract value getter to confirm, or you can show a transient 'pending' state until the read confirms the new stored value. Also consider debouncing UI updates if many events arrive quickly and batching state changes to avoid excessive re-renders. Security note: event logs are public — do not expose private or sensitive user data in events. Finally, include a small error-handling pathway: if parsing fails or BigNumber conversion throws, log the error and show a fallback UI element rather than crashing the app.

keyIdea.title: Parse and confirm
keyIdea.text: Convert BigNumbers, normalize addresses, and choose whether to optimistically update the UI or confirm via a storage read for critical state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › UI Processing
Parsing pipeline
1) Receive raw event object. 2) Convert BigNumber types to strings or numbers. 3) Normalize addresses. 4) Update UI state with optimistic or confirmed strategy. 5) Handle parse errors gracefully.
Example transform
{ setter: event.returnValues.setter,
  oldValue: event.returnValues.oldValue.toString(),
  newValue: event.returnValues.newValue.toString()
}
UI strategies
  • Optimistic: show the event value immediately, confirm later with a read.
  • Conservative: show a pending indicator until on-chain state is re-read.
  • Batch updates: group frequent events to reduce re-renders.
Error handling
If parsing fails, log the issue and display fallback UI. Never trust raw event data without conversion and sanity checks.

screens.title: Lab: Implement Real-time Listeners and Trigger Events
screens.subtitle: Follow the step-by-step terminal demo with Web3.js and Ethers.js

narration.text: This lab ties everything together. Start Ganache locally and deploy EventfulContract, then copy its ABI and address into your listener script. Create listenEvents. js with both a Web3. js WebSocket provider and an Ethers. js WebSocket provider configured to your Ganache WebSocket URL. In the Web3. js listener, subscribe to ValueChanged and OwnershipTransferred using contract. events. In the Ethers. js listener, subscribe to ValueChanged with contract. on and create a filter for OwnershipTransferred using contract. filters. Run listenEvents. js and keep it running in a terminal. In a second terminal or Remix, call setValue and transferOwnership to trigger events. Observe the console output: you should see the printed setter and the numeric values converted to readable strings, and filtered OwnershipTransferred events only for the address you passed to the filter. As you test, exercise safety practices: use WebSocket providers, convert numeric values with toString, unsubscribe after testing, and try simulating a disconnect to observe your reconnection logic. The goal of this hands-on segment is to produce a listener that reliably logs events, filters by indexed parameters, and cleans up when finished.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Deploy the contract locally, run a terminal listener with both Web3.js and Ethers.js, trigger events, and verify real-time output and filters.

narration.text: Remember these core ideas as you build real-time DApps. First, events are logged notifications stored in transaction logs; they are not a substitute for reading authoritative contract state. Second, use indexed parameters for values you will filter by; topics let nodes return matching logs efficiently. Third, prefer WebSocket providers for live subscriptions and implement unsubscribe and reconnection logic to keep listeners healthy. These three points cover the mechanics, efficiency, and operational safety you need to turn on-chain actions into responsive UI updates. Keep the habit of converting BigNumber numeric types before rendering and avoid placing sensitive data in events, since logs are public and permanent. Finally, use events for instant notifications and confirm critical state with direct reads when finality matters. Key Concepts means events = notifications; indexed = filterable; websocket + lifecycle management = reliable real-time updates.. In practical terms, core ideas to carry forward. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Events = notifications; indexed = filterable; WebSocket + lifecycle management = reliable real-time updates.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.5 › Key Concepts
Event (Solidity)
A mechanism for contracts to log information that external applications can listen to and query.
Indexed parameter
Marks up to three event fields as topics so nodes can efficiently filter matching logs.
WebSocketProvider
A persistent provider that enables real-time subscriptions to events and new blocks from an Ethereum node.
Summary

Use events and indexed parameters with a WebSocket provider, convert types for display, and manage subscriptions to build responsive, reliable DApps.

narration.text: Keep a quick checklist handy when you implement event-driven updates. First, always use a WebSocket provider for real-time subscriptions; HTTP does not stream. Second, index only the parameters you intend to filter by to save bandwidth and time. Third, implement unsubscribe and reconnection logic to avoid memory leaks and duplicate listeners. These three reminders help prevent the most common production issues when relying on contract events for UI updates. Quick Reference means websocket provider, index selectively, manage lifecycle with unsubscribe and reconnect.. In practical terms, three short reminders for implementation. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Implementation checklist
keyIdea.text: WebSocket provider, index selectively, manage lifecycle with unsubscribe and reconnect.

Use WebSocketProvider
Persistent connection required for real-time event streams and block subscriptions.
Index what you filter
